title: Lost mementos and his notched custom mouthpieces
summary: His handwritten parts, pictures and mouthpiece were thrown out; he had only two mouthpieces, filed and notched.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Too bad because those are of historic importance now, of course.
That's what I said, if you only knew that. You never know with the title. Many pictures too, different pictures we did away with.
Some musicians keep scrapbooks too, but hardly any of them save them very long. No. After their death they're usually thrown out or lost or somebody.

We kept them for quite a while, but after a few years past. My mother's got disgusted. Having that laying around there. And having a use for it. And we had to rid of them. At the corner of the mouthpiece was a steady machine drawing, then throwing somewhere else and I said, well throw it out. He had no use for it.
Did he put those notches on all of his mouthpieces? I mean even in his late years?
He saved it all the time.
Keep that in his pocket. Never put it down. Never leave it on his home. He treasured that thing.
Yes. But even the last mouthpiece he had, did he have those notches filed in?

Three notches he had on them. And then he used to take that hair file and go down there and just open that. Keep it clean. No, no it was to enlarge it. Enlarge it, make a bigger bore. At the bottom, but not on the top because he had, it was very small. He never did use just an ordinary mouthpiece. He said it was too wide and too heavy, you know, for him. And he'd always have it made. And after he had it made, well he'd fix it the way he wanted. He'd file and put the reedges on it. Yeah. And any time he'd sit down, he'd be working on that mouthpiece, you know, and look like, I don't know. He just treasured that thing. Yeah, yeah.
